title: Development charges by-laws adopted and public space bylaw ordered
subtitle: Long-term care reserve fund, 151 Bristol Street rezoning, and closed-session direction on tribunal appeals and encampments
overview: Council adopted the 2023 Development Charge Background Study and the 2024 Development Charge by-laws {{vote:m6}}. Charges will continue to be calculated city-wide for all services. Council also created a new development charge reserve fund for long-term care. These charges are how growth-related infrastructure is paid for, so they affect both housing costs and what the tax and rate base must cover.

Earlier in the day, after a closed session, council directed staff to draft a Public Space Use Bylaw on safety concerns about encampments and related activities on city-owned or operated land {{vote:m2}}. Staff are to bring it back by the end of February 2024. The mayor also reported that council gave staff direction on two Ontario Land Tribunal matters, at 140 Hadati Road and 78-82 Eastview Road. No details were released.

On the consent agenda, council approved a rezoning at 151 Bristol Street to allow two semi-detached buildings with additional residential dwelling units {{vote:m4}}. It also corrected the recorded vote result in the October 17, 2023 minutes {{vote:m5}}.

decisions.detail: Council approved the 2023 Development Charge Background Study as amended and the 2024 Development Charge by-laws, keeping a uniform city-wide approach {{vote:m6}}.
Council created a new Development Charge Reserve Fund for Long-Term Care and updated the General Reserve and Reserve Fund Policy to match.
Staff were directed to draft a bylaw addressing safety concerns about encampments and related activities on city lands, for council consideration by the end of February 2024 {{vote:m2}}.
Council approved a zoning change to permit two semi-detached buildings and additional residential dwelling units in Ward 3 {{vote:m4}}.
Council amended the October 17, 2023 planning minutes to correct the vote result for the 716 Gordon Street item {{vote:m5}}.

debate: A delegate argued that the gap between what development charges recover and the full cost of growth is funded by taxpayers. The delegate said this links to tax increases and that provincial changes under Bill 23 add to the public subsidy.

The delegate questioned who benefits, saying past reductions in charges have not lowered home prices. The delegate urged council to press the province or slow development approvals, and contrasted the subsidy with limited affordable housing funds.

Councillors asked whether the city has maximized what it may collect. Staff and consultants said the study followed provincial rules, took more than a year and a half with peer review meetings, and added services where possible.

Consultants said exemptions and limits on chargeable services mean developers do not pay the full cost of growth, and that the share varies with the type of building. They said Bill 23 has reduced what the city can collect.

On future provincial changes, consultants said the by-laws refer to the provincial act, so many changes would apply automatically. Council could reopen the by-laws at any time, likely without a formal reconsideration.
